Refined and Creative Vietnamese Cuisine
Aug 2026 • Solo
Thịt Đông Jelly Beef - I loved the variety of flavors in this dish and how every component had a role to play. There was also an interesting play on textures that made each bite more enjoyable. The beef flavor was persistent; even five minutes later, I could still taste it lingering on my tongue. The nước chấm also elevated the dish, providing just enough acidity to brighten the other flavors. 

Foie Gras Spring Roll - The filling was really soft and tender, although I wish the exterior had been crispier, especially since this was a spring roll. It wasn't very greasy. I liked the acidity that the mango brûlée brought to the dish. What impressed me most was that no single flavor dominated the bite. I could distinctly taste the foie gras, pork, herbs, and mango brûlée while still enjoying them together. This dish was well executed, and I would gladly ask for more rolls.

Le Petit Bánh Mì - This was a creative take on bánh mì, but I would still say a traditional bánh mì is better. The air baguette was almost entirely filled with pâté, so I thought the filling-to-bread ratio was excessive. It felt like 95% filling, with the bread mostly serving as a thin outer layer. I wanted more of that bread texture to balance the richness of the filling. Nonetheless, the dish itself was rich and flavorful.

Bánh Ram Ít Dumpling - This was really good and extremely savory, with a nice combination of softness and crunch. I could clearly taste the sticky rice, and despite all the seafood components, the dish wasn't overly salty. It wasn't greasy at all either. 

Crab & Asparagus - I could detect hints of both the crab and sea urchin, but I don't think their flavors came through strongly enough because the curry overpowered the seafood. As a result, the dish didn't feel as complex as I expected from its ingredients. The white asparagus, however, was fresh and slightly sweet, which complemented the natural sweetness of the crab.

Salmon Waffle Tart - I loved how aesthetically pleasing this dish was. I also liked that everything remained intact with every bite, especially since it took me at least three bites to finish it. The dill cream wasn't heavy; it was smooth and creamy, with enough tanginess to balance the saltiness of the smoked salmon and roe. The Vietnamese-French fusion was definitely evident here, particularly through the combination of bánh nhúng with the more classic French-inspired toppings.

Scallop & Sweet Corn - The sweetness in this dish was elegant and very well controlled. The scallop already provided its own natural sweetness, while the sauce wasn't overly sweet, keeping the overall sweetness at just the right level. Despite having several naturally sweet ingredients, the dish never became one-dimensional. 

Blue River Prawn - The prawn was juicy, succulent, and properly cooked. However, I was hoping for more of a smoky aroma or charred flavor from the grilling. The sauce was rich without being very salty and complemented the prawn. I also wish the young coconut noodles had been given more justice, as there were only around two or three strands on the plate, which wasn't really enough for me to appreciate the component properly. The pomelo was fresh and provided enough acidity to balance the richness of the dish.

Five Spice & Orange Duck - The duck was tender and juicy, with a strong and distinctive flavor. I also enjoyed the duck sausage, which was savory and had a nice charred quality. The sauce was peppery without being harsh, and there was enough of it to accompany the meat throughout the dish. Overall, I thought the sweet and savory elements were balanced.

Caviar Box - This was a surprising dish for me because I had never tried caviar with fruit and white chocolate before. Unfortunately, I wouldn't say the combination completely worked. The dish leaned heavily toward sweetness, while I was looking for more salinity from the caviar. I'm not sure whether the relatively mild salinity was characteristic of the particular Đà Lạt caviar used, but either way, the sweetness didn't complement the caviar well for me. It actually made me question whether the caviar needed to be there at all or whether its inclusion was more about adding a luxurious ingredient than improving the dish.

Since this is a Michelin-starred restaurant, I went into the meal with higher expectations and had a higher standard for each dish. That's why I was surprised to come away with only one favorite, which was the Bánh Ram Ít Dumpling, out of the ten dishes served. There were several dishes I enjoyed, and I still had a great experience dining here, but I was expecting more, given that this is Vietnam's first Michelin-starred restaurant.

The service, however, was great. The staff contributed positively to the experience. My main issue with the dining room itself was the spacing. The tables were positioned quite close together, and with other diners immediately to my left and right, I felt a little claustrophobic.

A few too many "buts"....
Aug 2026 • Family
We ordered from the a la carte menu and not one of those proposed. 
The premise is that the food isn't bad, but:
- some portions are truly of modest quantity
- the location is on a street where there is a permanent local market that isn't exactly elegant (personally, I didn't mind it, aside from a rat crossing the street, but it's still an aspect not to be underestimated, also in terms of prices)
- the dining rooms and the spacing are not appropriate for a restaurant of this type
- the table setting is practically absent
- the timing of the courses was not respected, dishes served without coordination for the table
- vegetarian dishes (except perhaps one) = "normal" menu dish - meat / fish (the balance?)
- staff willing and nice but not really professional
I won't go into the technical aspect of the cooking because I find that eating at least well is the minimum requirement, but you also go to a restaurant of this type for the overall experience and this, alas, was disappointing. 
Given what I've said, I must say that the price-to-quality ratio is definitely unbalanced considering we are in Vietnam, therefore with certain types of costs for staff, rent, raw materials, etc. I reiterate that I didn't eat anything bad; a little more organization, a few dollars less, and a little more attention to some aspects that I understand require energy and effort would suffice, and I think we would start to get there...

Incredible food, but rushed like an assembly line
Jun 2026 • Couples
My experience here was a heartbreaking contradiction. On one hand, the kitchen is executing at an elite level; on the other, the front-of-house team is running the dining room like a high-speed assembly line.
Let’s start with the positives: the food was absolutely phenomenal. Every single dish across the 10-course degustation menu was beautifully conceptualized, technically flawless, and bursting with flavor. The kitchen team clearly possesses immense talent and deserves recognition for what they put on the plate.
Unfortunately, the service entirely derailed the evening. Despite paying a premium price for a high-end dining experience, we were treated less like individual guests and more like cattle being herded through a system. Because the restaurant serves the degustation concurrently, we were forced into the exact same rhythm as everyone else in the room. There was zero personalization or attentiveness to our pace. Waitstaff were constantly hovering, aggressively trying to clear our plates before we had even finished our last bites. It felt less like a relaxed, luxurious dinner and more like a race against a stopwatch.
To make matters worse, the matching wine pairing was a complete letdown. The pours were incredibly small—bordering on stingy—and offered absolutely no value for the steep price tag attached to them.
To top off a frustrating night, a hefty mandatory service charge was tacked onto the bill. Forced tipping is hard to swallow at the best of times, but when a meal is already expensive and the service is this rushed and impersonal, it feels like an insult.
If you only care about what is on the plate, the food won't disappoint. But if you expect a premium price tag to come with premium hospitality, respect for your time, and a relaxed atmosphere, you will likely leave feeling as ripped off as we did.

Fantastic Return
Jun 2026 • Solo
Returning to ANAN Saigon - @anansaigon - after a year, I was struck by how the restaurant continues to master the delicate art of evolution without alienation. Nestled within the gritty, pulsating heart of the Chợ Cũ market, the iconic “tube house” setting remains a masterclass in atmospheric contrast—a polished, vibrant sanctuary that feels entirely at home amidst the city’s chaotic energy.

@petercuongfranklin Chef Peter Cuong Franklin’s “Cuisine Mới” philosophy is on full display here. What remains most impressive is the unwavering consistency in his vision: an ability to deconstruct and elevate the soul of Vietnamese street culture through a sophisticated, refined lens. Every course is a testament to his deep respect for local roots, where the heritage of the flavors is never lost, even as they are reimagined through modern technique.

The service is warm, knowledgeable, and distinctly convivial, mirroring the unpretentious spirit of Saigon itself. It is a rare, high-octane dining experience that manages to be both intellectually stimulating and deeply comforting. 

ANAN remains a vital pulse in Vietnam’s gastronomic scene, proving that true culinary innovation is about honoring the past with every forward-thinking bite. A triumphant return.

5-stars!
Apr 2026 • Couples
Anan Saigon is certainly expensive by local standards, but when you consider it’s a full tasting menu at a 1-Michelin star restaurant for roughly $100 USD per person, it feels like a fantastic value. We made a reservation for two several weeks in advance via email and the process was incredibly easy.

The restaurant is tucked into the middle of the market area just off central District 1, within walking distance of the Reverie Saigon where we were staying. Anan occupies a narrow traditional Saigon-style home converted into a multi-level dining space, with the restaurant on the lower floors and their related cocktail bar, Nhau Nhau, upstairs. The whole place has a stylish, energetic vibe while still feeling intimate and distinctly local.

Service was polished to Western fine dining standards, which makes sense given that many of the diners appeared to be international visitors. Every member of the staff spoke fluent English and explained each dish thoughtfully and clearly.

We chose the Saigon tasting menu, which began with amuse-bouche bites before progressing through seven courses plus dessert. The standout for me was the “Le Petit Banh Mi” — a playful bite-sized interpretation of Vietnam’s iconic sandwich, filled with pâté and beef while still delivering the crispiness you expect from a proper baguette. Creative, delicious, and memorable. I also loved the Ha Noi turmeric fish. The cod was cooked perfectly, with the sweetness of the fish balancing beautifully against the earthy turmeric and flavorful sauce.

Dessert was outstanding. As someone who loves Vietnamese coffee, I thought the combination of robusta coffee bitterness, chocolate, and coconut jelly was incredibly well executed. The textures and flavors all complemented each other beautifully.

The cocktail menu also looked very inventive, and I imagine that creativity extends upstairs to Nhau Nhau bar. Unfortunately we didn’t have time to visit, but I definitely would on a future trip.

While Anan is undeniably a splurge for Vietnam, the creativity, execution, service, and overall experience make it absolutely worth it for travelers looking for a memorable dining experience in Saigon. There are not many places in the world where you can enjoy a Michelin-starred tasting menu of this caliber for around $100 USD per person.

Superb food, average atmosphere and service for the $$$
Mar 2026 • Couples
We were keen to visit one of the many Micheline star restaurants across Vietnam as part of our trip and Anan Saigon came highly recommended. We pre-booked the Chef's tasting menu with wine pairing - $230 per person.

The restaurant is location in one of Ho Chi Minh's wet markets so an interesting walk to find it. The restaurant itself is located across the florrs of an old residential style building so lots of very small rooms. We were early so started with a coktail at Nhau Nhau on the roof - which also serves some of the tasting menu disches as a la carte options. Cocktail options were limited but interesting, however my husbands drink was served in a plastic glass which is a little naff for a michelin restaurant.

We were then taken downstairs t the restaurant - a small, very modern room with maybe 10-12 tables - a little cramped and close together and lacking the atmosphere I expected. The staff explained the concept of the tasting menu and went to collect our first course. When the first course was served we had to remind the staff that we also wanted the wine pairing even though it was clearly noted on our reservation. 

The food is incredibly prepared - stunning to look at, great interpretations of classic vietnamese dishes and in most cases not what we would order in a restaurant so a great chance to try different dishes. The pase the dishes are served is good and the staff are very passionate about the dishes and describing the region that influences them, the chefs preperation style and how best to enjoy them.

In summary - it was a good experience but not great and for the extortionate price being charged it should be great. The atmosphere in the restaurant is sterile - it feels like a dentist waiting room, not a restaurant. The staff are good but not great - we were never asked if wanted other drinks, our package should have included a desert cocktail which never arrived and we were interrogated if we didnt finish a dish! There is a lot of choice across Vietnam if you want to visit a Michelin star restauant and I'm not sure this is the best there is to try?

Maybe I had expectations that were too high. Maybe I didn’t. Either way, this New Year’s Eve dinner was below all criticism. The first thing we were met with, after being shown to our table, was an unset table (completely empty) and a waiter who, when I asked about the password, let out a big sigh. Yes, dealing with customers can be tiring, I know—but try not to show it.
After that, things became confusing. Even though we had pre-ordered a menu, the waiter wanted us to order from a different one. That was probably just due to language difficulties. The napkins looked like mine do when I take them out of the dryer—slightly wrinkled and unironed. Not everyone owns a mangle; I certainly don’t.
The food was mediocre, and the poor service continued throughout the entire evening. I would have liked to leave the restaurant after ten minutes, but my family insisted that we stay. And perhaps it was good that we did. The food was nothing special—and considering the price per person, it was simply not acceptable.
Will I go here again? Nope.
Will I recommend it? Nope.
Do I understand how they got a star? Nope.

Jan 2026 • Family
Despite the Michelin star and high expectations, our dinner at Anan Saigon was a complete failure and frankly alarming.

We dined here last night as a group of four people. Unfortunately, two out of four of us suffered from clear symptoms of food poisoning shortly after the meal. Nausea, stomach cramps, and vomiting followed, completely ruining the evening and the day after.

What makes this even more disturbing is that later at our hotel we ran into the table that had been seated behind us at the restaurant. Out of their group of three, one person also became sick with food poisoning. This strongly suggests that our case was not isolated.

For a restaurant that proudly holds one Michelin star, this level of food safety failure is unacceptable. No culinary creativity, storytelling, or fine presentation can compensate for making guests ill. Food safety should be the absolute minimum standard, and here it was clearly not met.

A wonderful dining experience with a creative interpretation of Vietnamese street food
Sep 2024 • Couples
Anan
We enjoyed a beautiful, intimate dinner at Anan Saigon where the customer service, quality, presentation and most importantly the taste of the food was absolutely worthy of the Michelin star that has been awarded to the venue.

Starting with the customer service, we were warmly greeted by our lovely host Thao who looked after us for the whole night. I had originally booked the rooftop table but due to the rain forecast that evening Thao had thoughtfully moved us to a cosy table next to the bar where we enjoyed the show throughout the evening as the resident bartender mixed up a variety of cocktail concoctions. 

Thao struck that perfect balance where she was attentive to our needs while not being intrusive, checked to make sure that we were happy throughout the evening, shared her recommendations when we asked for her opinion, and ensured that we had a wonderful experience.

We ordered the following dishes:
* Salmon Waffle - consisting of a Banh Nhung waffle tart, smoked salmon, crème fraiche, salmon roe. This was a delightful start to our evening. The waffle tart was delicate with a lovely crunch. The smoked salmon and crème fraiche combined beautifully for a balanced, creamy, smoky salmon flavour hit, broken up by little explosions of salmon hits from the salmon roe.
* Hà Nội Tumeric Fish - perfectly cooked Black Cod sitting on top of a flavoursome tumeric foam with hints of dill, garnished with a bun noodle on the side. The Black cod literally melted in our mouths, the tumeric foam was not overpowering and just complimented the fish and the bun noodle and dill cracker provided a variety of different textures. A wonderful experience and arguably our favourite dish of the evening, noting that every dish we had was a winner.
* Seafood spring roll - Crispy spring roll with crab, shrimp and pork, fresh herbs, Nuoc Cham sauce. A beautifully executed spring roll. The filling was tasty, soft and flavourful, surrounded by a delicate, flaky, crispy skin. Once again, different textures combined beautifully for arguably one of the loveliest, high end spring rolls I have ever eaten.
* Crab Fried Rice - Camau crab, shrimp, pork, spring onion, garlic, onsen egg. Served in a claypot with the ingredients proudly displayed, the first thing to do is mix it all up. There were just so many flavours and textures to enjoy. The softness of the crab meat, firmness of the pork Chinese sausage with bits of crunchiness mixed in for good measure.
* Grilled Squid - Chargrilled squid served with mango cucumber salad, green herb chilli sauce. Not sure how they did it but the squid had a wonderful char flavour while at the same time had a melt in the mouth texture. How they managed to do this with squid is beyond me. No rubber texture here.
* Roast Duck Street Style Pizza - Confit Mekong duck, mozzarella, fresh herbs, tamarind and hoisin sauce, grilled rice paper. Take the best Peking duck pancake that you have ever eaten and multiply it by a wow factor of 10. The duck was so tender and full of flavour that Donald Duck would be proud. The herbs were well balanced and worked in harmony with the duck meat. The sliced cucumber provided bursts of freshness. But what I really loved was the grilled rice paper “pizza base” that while so delicate that you would think it would shatter if you breathed on it, was more than up for the task of supporting the delicious pizza payload. And upon biting into it the crunch was oh so satisfying. Along with the Hà Nội Tumeric Fish, this was my favourite dish of the night.
* Fish sauce ice cream - Vanilla, fish sauce caramel, Phu Quoc pepper, Nuoc Mam perfume. The vanilla bean ice cream was so creamy and the fish sauce caramel was an interesting and delicious take on classic salted caramel. The Nuoc Mam perfume in its own perfume bottle was a a very nice touch but my recommendation is to spray your dessert sparingly as it is quite strong and fragrant.
* Young coconut caviar - Young coconut ice cream, Dakar Caviar. The coconut ice cream provided a sweet creamy flavour contrasted by the saltiness of the caviar. The small mint leaves provided a strong punch of minty flavour. 

We also ordered the Pho-jito cocktail which was essentially the essence of pho captured in a cocktail. A very interesting concoction indeed. 

The head chef Peter Cuong also paid us a visit during our meal and was very warm, personable and passionate about his food. A really lovely guy who picked my Sydney accent immediately. 

So thank you Anan for a wonderful dining experience. Absolutely one of our top dining highlights in Ho Chi Minh City. Highly recommended.

My wife and I were in HCMC for a week and we decided to treat ourselves to a nice restaurant for NYE. After seeing the reviews for Anan we booked in September as we expected that what is rated as "Vietnam's Best" would be booked out. We were advised that the Chef's Tasting Menu would start at six and there were no other available times so assumed that it would be a lengthy fourteen course dinner after which we would go to the roof top bar and watch the fireworks as we welcomed the New Year. What could go wrong?

Upon entering Anan we were greeted and shown to the upstairs bar/dining room which had seating capacity of 15. There were two diners in it. On NYE. In Vietnam's "Best Restaurant". But cool we were early and pretty soon the place would fill up...except that it didn't.

Ordered our pre-dinner cocktails and got ourselves ready for long and relaxed evening of good food and interesting wine but then the first course appeared almost immediately followed by course two and three in quick succession before our pre-dinner cocktails had been made by the barman standing in front of us. 

Why the haste? Was there another cover that night that we didn't know about? No there wasn't however the wait staff appeared to be in rush to get the courses out even if the diners didn't have a drink.

As for the food? Some was OK including the Cha Ca La Vong (Black Cod) and the Ca Phe Su'a (Chocalte mousse) but the rest was pretty disappointing and even bland. We tasted much better food in our stay in Vietnam and at much cheaper prices then Anan.

The real problem is with the service. The staff on our level spent so much time in the hallway next to the dining room on their phones rather than looking after the diners who are paying USD 100 per person for the privilege. One of our fellow diners (remember there are four of us in total on this floor) had to actually get up from her chair and find someone to turn the AC up. I had to refill my water from my own water bottle as there was no one around to look after the customers. 

It wasn't a case of them be snowed under by a workload as there were only four of us!

At 7:30 two gentlemen came in for dinner and the 50% surge in patronage caused us to be rewarded by three bar men appearing to do goodness knows what as the first two customers left not long afterwards. Meanwhile the course came out in quick succession (an average of one every 8 minutes or so) so not much time for enjoyment and discussion.

The last three courses all turned up at about the same time and we were out in under two hours. For a 14 course dinner!

I think that the best way to sum up this place is that the decor has a number of pretty nice vintage Vietnamese record sleeves on the wall and a cool vintage turntable behind behind the bar but near the end of our time the music fell silent...because it's delivered by a tablet under the turntable and no staff were around to restart until five or ten minutes later when one of the staff graced us with their presence. A restaurant that looks good on the surface but underneath it's pretty hopeless.

This was by far the most expensive place we ate at in Vietnam and by far the most disappointing not only on a value basis but just the basic food equation of it not being very good. The terrible service was simply an added "bonus"...

Save yourself the time and money and avoid this place. There are simply much better options.

The “frose” was a slushy type thing but served in a tall glass with no way to drink until it was melted into a liquid, a straw or something would have made sense, the consumption of the cocktail was obviously not taken into account. 

We had the “white fish” ceviche. It was delicious; large portion with lots of fish, we were impressed. There was a type of seafood in the ceviche that we had never had before. It had a very different texture that the other fish. We saved a piece so we could ask the server what it was. We are adventurous eaters and it was exciting to have tried something new. The server said “it’s white fish. It says on the menu”. Okay.. we are chefs and we knew this was not the same as the other white fish in the dish. He continued to ask other servers and even the kitchen and came back to re confirm that it was in fact white fish and implied that we had not paid attention while reading the menu. We were able to go online and read some reviews about the dish from previous diners and learned that it was actually jellyfish. Very disappointed that the servers have are not briefed on what ingredients are in each dish. 

The ban xeo tacos were quite good but the crepe broke into many pieces immediately after taking one bite. The carpaccio had no salt, and the meat was cut very thick and was hard to eat. Nothing about the dish stood out. The silken tofu was quite tasty. 

For our mains we shared the banana blossom and duck salad as well as the bone marrow. The salad was fine. The bone marrow was supposed to be served with a pho pesto. It came with a small watercress salad, some thinly sliced shallots, and 3 very small pieces of bread. The salad was dressed but the greens were not dry so the dressing didn’t stick. There was no pho pesto and a ton of cheap truffle oil poured over the top(which was not mentioned on the description of the dish). There was 0 seasoning and no pesto? We asked about the pesto and the sever clearly understood and said she would ask then immediately changed her mind and said I don’t understand what you are saying and walked away. 

We had a delicious coffee martini and the worlds smallest and most expensive scoop of vanilla ice cream, it was delicious and had a nice fish sauce to spritz on top. 

Overall the food was fairly pleasant but we were treated so horribly by all the service staff I can’t fathom giving them more than 1 star. Unacceptable for a restaurant charging these prices. We left feeling unwelcome and that we had been ripped off. 

Don’t waste your money. You can get better food for $2 anywhere on the streets and feel more welcome.

My friends dressed up for the dinner, but soon realised that it was not necessary the moment we stepped in. We saw other patrons dressed in berms and slippers (I did tee shirt with long joggers and shoes). It was also interesting to find that almost all the other patrons seated on the ground floor with us appeared to be Singaporeans too. I think that kind of took away the magic of "authenticity" with regards to the Vietnamese experience a bit.

We ordered the 9-course tasting menu (980,000++ VND per pax), and added an additional appetiser (beef flank wrapped in betel leaf).

I was disappointed to find that they served each course as a plate to be shared by 2 persons. As we were a party of 5, it was an odd number, which meant one person (ie. me) was served an individual portion. It was still fine, until the last main (fried rice) was served. The 2-pax serving came with a poached egg to be broken and mixed into the rice, whereas my individual portion did not get served with any poached egg.

I asked them why my bowl of rice did not come with a poached egg, and the crew tried to explain that my bowl of rice had more egg stir-fried into it (?!?). I mean, come on.

I did enjoy the flavours of the food served, and really liked the Chicken Banana Blossom salad the most. Perhaps the least to be desired was the Coconut Lime Sorbet, which was served in the middle of all the courses. They had probably pre-prepared the scoops of sorbet in a bowl and stored them in a freezer. It was frozen solid. I tried to use my spoon to break some off the lump, but the scoop of sorbet jumped off the bowl and landed on the floor. There, it laid for rather long (when I was about to finish my fried rice?) before it started showing signs of melting.

My wife and I decided to go for the Sai gon tasting menu, one of three tasting options.

You start with two Appetisers; Banh Xeo Tacos (shrimp & pork tacos dressed with fresh herbs and with peanut dipping sauce) and Chicken banana blossom (chicken, rau ram, banana blossom, cabbage, mint, peanuts and crispy shallots). 

After a short break, they then serve teo second courses; Nem Nuong pork skewers (grilled pork sausage, vermicelli and pork & peanut sauce) and a roast duck delat pizza (duck, mozzarella, shallots and mustard greens on a thin crust pizza bread). Both were particularly memorable.

Then they served the main course; Saigon shaking beef (tenderloin with tomato, watercress, bell peppers and shallots) with crab fried rice (fried rice with crab, garlic and a whole fried egg on top).

We then requested that they served our two included desserts on their rooftop terrace/bar. A great idea.

First came a Creme brûlée (caramel custard with banana, Dalat strawberries, passion fruit and mint) then imaginatively presented Cotton candy /candy floss, which was Tamarind, coffee and chocolate flavoured.

Topped off with a couple of cocktails it was s great night and I'd highly recommend.

Wanted to love it, actually quite disappointing
Jul 2019 • Friends
Let me first start by saying that I was excited to eat at this restaurant and I say this with the intent of giving constructive feedback as well as sharing potential consumer awareness. 

We had the chef’s tasting menu with wine pairing, and two cocktails to start. We have been in Vietnam for only a week and had some of the most amazing cuisine, meeting and exceeding many of our expectations at commonly humble locations. Therefore, we had high expectations and were excited to experience refinement in this cuisine. Unfortunately, this meal had not come close to offering what we had hoped. I’ll do my best to break the components down in order to offer feedback. 

We started with cocktails: the menu sounded unique and interesting. We had the coffee negroni and the phohito. Though beautiful presentation, the phohito lacked flavour and fragrance. Having had a few pho flavoured cocktails in Vietnam it lacked that flavours of fresh herbs; known in Vietnam, and spice: cinnamon, star anise and chilli. The Coffee negroni lacked any bitterness from the Campari of a good negroni was over powered by over roasted coffee. 

The menu:

Amuse bouche - smoked soft boiled quails egg with salmon roe: beautifully presented on a nest of smoking hay, smell of tea leaves. Soft yolk but lacked seasoning (a common theme throughout the meal) and the smokiness quickly dissipated once the dish was presented. Even the salmon roe was lost in the bite. Wanted more smokiness with the creaminess of the yoke.

Starters - Caviar Congee: probably the most balanced dish of the evening. The sturgeon caviar complimented the rich egg yolk well and the texture profile of the crispy rice gave it a good mouth feel. My only comment is that it’s the second rich egg dish in as many courses. 

Flower Crab with pomelo: another beautifully presented dish, served on sea salt in the crab shell with sesame seed and rice cracker. The cracker itself was a little stale. Dish again under season and the pomelo lacked the citrus note we wanted from the dish. Lacked the combination of sweet crab meat, tart citrus and saltiness from the sea that we were hoping for. 

Banh Xeo tacos: Banh Xeo is a great dish combining crispy rice pancake, sometimes seafood and/or pork with bean sprouts. Though, I understand what the idea of the dish, it feels like a crude fusion dish that misses the charm and flavour of the original. More of a mince pork taco with a prawn on it, again lacking seasoning. 

As a note we had our first of only 2 glasses of wine in the flight here. I’m unsure of the actual wine but tasted like a New Zealand Sav Blanc which didn’t really suit any of the first dishes. 

Moving to the main dishes - Water buffalo carpaccio: again under seasoned and completely overpowered by the rich quail egg yolk, and truffle with no tart notes to cut through the richness. There’s a mustard leaf that is commonly served in Vietnam, that could have really shone here. And I’m a believer that though truffle is delicious, it’s powerful, and can completely overpower a dish. I’d emphasise that even though there are expensive ingredients available, it doesn’t mean they necessarily compliment a dish. 

Note, the second glass of wine was served here, I think it was a Gamay and though can be served cold, it didn’t work here and would have tasted better served room temperature. Again didn’t really suit the dishes. 

Fois Gras imperial roll: initially, I though this might be a take on the Banh Mi, it turned out to be a fried spring roll. With anything fried it can be hard to not loose the flavour of the content of the dish. Though crispy, the dish lost any flavour of the fois gras; another example of expensive ingredients used without thought in my opinion. No citrus notes to cut through. The greasiness also meant you lost the delicate flavour of the herbs served in accompaniment. A poor dish in my view. 

Betel leaf with brisket: I liked this dish, the meat was delicate served with a sweet soy, maybe garlic notes but again a little under seasoned. The peanuts worked well.

Deconstructed pho (spherified, served on spoon): lacked nearly any seasoning apart from the salted beef on top. Felt like a gimmick without the flavour to back the presentation. I wanted an umami bomb, we got an unflavoured water bomb. 

Wagyu pho: once again very under seasoned, I found myself reaching for the bottle of sriracha to season the dish. Sacrilege maybe but lacked nearly any flavour. On a positive note the texture of the beef was amazing. The bone marrow could have done with a few more minutes under the salamander, but quite disappointing from a restaurant that prides itself on the $100 pho. I say for now to save your money and find a place round the corner if you are considering this. 

Dessert

Deconstructed lime - lime ice cream lacking any citrus and a green chocolate shell which provided texture, but added nothing to the overall flavour of the dish. Looks interesting. Tasty? Not so much.

Cotton candy - coffee and chocolate was taste good, mocha cotton candy was great. Tamarind and cheese; I would suggest to avoid, especially in a dessert. The pears served with the dish were flavourless: in general most Vietnamese fruit is full of flavour; these pears were very bland.

In conclusion, the setting is sophisticated, but the dinning experience was quite disappointing, especially at this price point. Nearly all the dishes lacked flavour and seasoning. In fact, it’s quite expensive for what it’s offering given that you can get amazing dishes at nearly 100th of the price, and sadly I can’t say it’s worth it. And I feel there’s a tendency of using expensive ingredients without much thought about how they enhance the dishes, rather more of a talking point to sell the menu. I wanted to to be excited about this restaurant but feel it has a long way to go. Though, maybe this might seem unfair to some, I have tried to be fair and constructive. For now, save your money, and enjoy the amazing Vietnamese cuisine that you can get at a significantly less price tag.

After the drinks are served, a well-presented meat dish is served. This platter is left on the table until the actual brewing pot that contains all the meat and soup base is brought out. Next, a simple bowl that contains only three pieces of meat is brought out. It isn’t any typical meat found in any supermarket but instead, it is truffle wagyu beef. Even though it took some time, the final course finally was brought out, containing the remaining seven types of different beef. The beef platter that was brought in the beginning was dipped in the pot and cooked. The quality and taste of the soup was magnificent. As the whole meal is set out in front of me I was very amused by the presentation for it made the meal looked scrumptiously tasty. But, as I asked the waiter why the meal was a bit salty they said that it was because of the bones of the beef that was cooked for the soup. I suggest that if you are a person who doesn’t eat a lot of salt, you should order a side of hot boiled water to add it to the soup. 
This particular meal is a bit expensive and I don’t suggest customers on a budget to eat here. But, if you are willing to spend your money to enjoy this meal then it is worth it. In addition, not only was the restaurant a nice place, and the fine food they served, the service there was exceptionally well. The waiters would normally check up on their customers and periodically take away the dishes that were finished by their customers. Comparing to other Vietnamese restaurants that I have been too, I think this is one of the best restaurants I have been introduced to. If you are not interested in this type of meal the restaurant also provides other different kinds of grilled courses and soup based courses. Anan restaurant - Modern Saigon's reflection from the Tradition
Sep 2018 • Friends
I love traveling and food and I think I have visited almost every good restaurant in Saigon, all the bars, diners and fun places this enchanting city has to offer. Since my friend Quynh was back from Australia, a fun-filled girls night out was mandatory for us.  Rolling down the list of all the places I have visited and the ones that are left, I decided to try Anan Restaurant and Rooftop Bar.

The location was a bit unexpected since it is located at 89 Ton That Dam Street, District 1, which is the oldest market area of Saigon. Anan was tucked away a little deep in the old market area in District 1 but trying this restaurant out was similar to finding hidden treasure in the deep seas. The street was packed and crowded with steep apartments and we had to take a long walk up to the concrete stairways, where Anan was hidden away. There are not much cafes or restaurants in the old market area and Anan stands out really well because of its stylish look. Your eye would not miss as it is an extremely chic place.

Anan rooftop bar with Anan original cacktails!
All ready for a girls night out, me and my best friend Quynh, set off a little early at around 6 pm in hope to see a little more of the city on our way to the restaurant. As we got there, Quynh wanted some shots right away to blend in with the chilly atmosphere first so we directly made our way up to the rooftop bar. I have seen many rooftop bars in Saigon that reveal a mesmerizing view of this breathtaking city but Anan had a very unique view laid in front of us since the area it is located in, has the urban charm of the city with tall buildings and colorful lights.

Coming down to the food and trying the cuisine Anan was known for, it is certain that this restaurant takes the lead in modern Vietnamese cuisine. Anan Saigon offered us unconventional food such as Vietnamese with Italian, Vietnamese with Mexican etc. I have never heard of Mexican Tacos with Pho flavor before. Although, I have tried Vietnamese egg Bánh xèo tacos, Bò Kho beef stew tacos and Pho rolls I was certainly not expecting such an incredible fusion of Vietnamese and Mexican food.

Mexican Tacos Met Vietnamese Food
I was highly impressed by how innovative their cooking style and skills were. The food portions were small but marvelous except the Dalat-style pizza. It was somewhat alright, not that good. Their cocktails were very exquisite, we tried Old Market Mai Tai with fresh mints and fruits and it tasted heavenly and refreshing.

Since we went a little earlier, we enjoyed the happy hour up at the bar. We found a small sitting area for smaller groups like ours to have a couple of drinks on the back side. Remember to make a reservation in advance since the place was jam-packed in less than half an hour. No wonder they get quite a lot of customers. The staff was well-informed about the cuisine on the menu and the chef did an amazing job with the mixing of traditional and modern Vietnamese cuisine to a unique level.

To sum it all up and put an end to this great night, we also ordered white wine which was equally as refreshing. Had a couple of their famous cocktails and went home happy. The restaurant is a must if you are a foodie like me because we had a great time!

One giant leap for Vietnamese food!
Apr 2018 • Couples
CONGRATULATIONS, ănăn and chef Peter!! You've transformed Vietnamese food!

Having experienced so many restaurants in Vietnam for over 15 years, I had come to the conclusion that Vietnamese food was dedicated to staying "basic", traditional, in the original state. And from cheap to mid-range, in terms of pricing.
So many disappointing experiences (still today in 2018) in supposedly upscale restaurants, finally serving the same common dishes at triple, quadruple prices, almost exclusively to tourists. Besides, sometimes at lower quality, food and service wise.

And then I came to ănăn with my wife, on a quiet evening. We had an amazing time there, a 95% flawless experience (always room for improvement!).
ănăn is a game changer in Vietnamese cuisine. If you know all your basics in Vietnamese food, come try ănăn and you'll have new sensations, you'll feel complexity in and subtlety of flavours that only fine dining offers. This is fine dining, what ănăn has achieved!

Our evening couldn't start better, because we were greeted by chef Peter himself. And thank you for your advice, Peter; instead of ordering a large plate that would have been too much for 2, we opted to taste more small dishes. A festival of flavours!
Beforehand, we spent an hour on the rooftop to enjoy happy hours and the gorgeous view.
Unavoidable appetizer to a culinary journey :)

We had:
- Bánh Xèo Tacos, Shrimp & Pork (2 pieces): tastes exactly like bánh xèo, in a much finer execution, with the great additional crunchy touch
- Betel Leaf Beef (2 pieces): the most tantalizing dish on the picture - phenomenal burst of flavours, wrapped in a lovely seasoned purple lettuce leaf (the smoky feeling is intense!)
- Foie Gras Imperial Roll (4 pieces): specially recommended by Peter - another burst of flavours, where the foie gras is clearly noticeable (the unknown sensation to eat French & Vietnamese food at the same time!)
- Đà Lạt Pizza, Escargot: also recommended by Peter - wow, cheese in Vietnamese food! if you're a fan of ốc (snails), don't miss it, great for 2
- Broken Lime: a masterpiece of a dessert - beautiful, perfect balance between the acidity of lime and the spiciness of ginger snap
plus the signature Trà Đá cocktail, delicious and ideal to enhance all these tasty dishes.

We can't wait to come back, already, and to try other splendours of the menu.
We liked everything: the food, the place, the atmosphere (lively but not noisy), the friendly & efficient service (in the restaurant and on the rooftop).
We don't understand the few critics of some grumpy reviewers.
This isn't expensive for what is served. We paid about 1M vnd for 2, a la carte (without wine, though). 1/3 or 1/4 of what we usually pay at La Villa, the longtime reference for French fine dining in Saigon, where we're regulars.
This is fine dining. For this price, we get mediocre food in a common place in Paris (my hometown). Same in London, NY, etc. Nowhere else in the world, you can eat ănăn's food.

This restaurant is a treat for visitors, locals and expats. No equivalent in town.
We recommend couples to order small dishes, as we did, to experience as many flavours as possible. Large plates are better shared between 3 or more people.
Undoubtedly, the 4 tasting menus are great deals for groups, as we could observe.
Since we saw the table of 3 next to us having one dish each, I want to tell tourists, who might read this review, that Vietnamese food is to be shared. It's a pity to eat one's portion in one's corner and not to try anything else! 

Again, congratulations to Peter and his team. Marvelous work!
We hope to join the 1 Year Anniversary Party!

I read about Peter Coung , the chef behind this restaurant and his vast experience in finance and food ( founding chef behind viet kitchen, Chom Chom in Hong Kong ) is as varied and distinguished as the food I ate here on Sunday 8/4/18.

It was a fitting finale for a great dinner after a month in Vietnam travelling from North to south pursuing my passion of food , photography and meeting Vietnamese people . Along this journey I ate some very good food from street food to restaurants but Anan was the restaurant where I ate the most memorable food in my one month in Vietnam. 

I made a booking via email and got a reply promptly . 

Anan is situated right in the heart of district one close to bitexco tower and Ben Thanh Market. This restaurant is spread over 5 stories with a rooftop bar and is situated on a road where there is a wet market . I found this interesting as I walked past looking at the fresh vegetables , herbs and meats at the stalls before I reached Anan. 

I find the food menu interesting ( varied and sufficient to satiate all tastes including vegetarians without being enclopaedic ). The drinks menu is comprehensive.

I ordered King Mushroom on skewers ( grilled mushrooms, lemongrass , sesame soy and garlic ), Dalat pizza 🍕 pepperoni ( 
Dalat chorizo, tomato sauce , mozzarella cheese , scarmorza and herbs 🌿) and Saigon shaking beef 🥩 ( Australian beef tenderloin , watercress , cherry tomatoes , shallots and bell peppers and garlic ).

I drank a phojito cocktail 🍸( fragrant sticky rice wine , sugar , lime juice and pho herbs ) and a craft beer ( IPA brewed by Pasteur Street Brewery ) . I like the phojito which can be Anan’s signature cocktail. It has a grilled star anise and a grilled / charred cinnamon stick and a chilli on top And lemongrass in the cocktail. These are the exact ingredients used for making the pho broth . I used the charred cinnamon stick to stick up my phojito . It’s tastes great with hints of pho broth . Yummy 😋. The IPA beer was very bitter and was a good match to cleanse your palate . 

The grilled mushrooms were very tasty 😋 and whetted my Appetite for the dishes to follow . The Dalat pizza was served on a wooden platter with the pizza cut up so you can pick up with chopsticks 🥢. A first for me . Peter’s version of pizza works for me . The pizza base is super thin and crispy and the whole bite size just fills your mouth . The Saigon shaking beef is just sublime . The tenderloin is tender and cooke to perfection . All the ingredients in this dish works well together but for me the water cress ( I suspect it’s raw or quickly blanched in boiling water ) elevates this dish to another level . The soft crunch adds texture . One thing I noticed is the generous use of small green peppercorns. It’s adds a mild peppery taste . The green peppercorns was not listed in the ingredients . 

I enjoyed my dinner tremendously and will be back to eat my way through the menu . I am longing to try the deluxe pho ( truffle wagyu pho 🍲).

I went up to the rooftop bar to take some photos of the HCM landmarks which are lighted up beautifully at night . The bar is coZy and intimate . 

Service was good and the 3 different waitresses I dealt with all spoke good English and they opened the sliding doors for me . 

This restaurant is highly remembered for its inspiring food .

My family loved a beer in the street as they waited for their table and the night we went together, we went to a small local bar that sold craft beer, I had a locally brewed cider actually, before heading back to Anan.
On being seated we, I think luckily, had a table just inside the door, in full view of all the evening market life, as well as the huge wet season deluge that followed a little later.
This is not the cheapest eatery in town, but the approach to all dishes is innovative, with almost witty references to traditional local cuisine, all dishes using fresh ingredients, delicious and attractively presented.
We enjoyed every dish we chose, but maybe we lent towards the sumptuous pork chop, superbly cooked, leaving the sliced pork looking a little like tender sushi and I think our party individually each counted in our heads, how many slices we each had and weighed up quietly whether, if we had another slice, would we be the greedy one. 
My family are keen cooks and were interested in the process of cooking that made the pork dish so delicious and tender and really appreciated when the chef came to our table to share his skills and knowledge.
We drank Pasteur Brewing Company beer, enjoying once again locally crafted beer, that is now internationally recognized.
I would argue against a recent article I read, which stated the best food was being served inside local hotels, nominating Anan as a prime example of literally eating out, so close to where many ingredients were sourced and the vibrant life HCMC is known for.

Atmosphere: The rooftop is one of the main attractions but there is a lot more. The restaurant and bar carry a casual metropolitan vibe where you can either eat sitting or standing almost anywhere in the venue. The elegant feel is made accessible by the range of seating and an intimate yet inclusive space that facilitates great interactions between strangers and between guests and the staff. The seats outside amongst the seller vendors in the market and observe daily commerce and pedestrians are a true feature to experience. Sometimes the rooftop can get crowded but it doesn't feel cramped and is always fun- more like a friend's rooftop bbq in summer in Brooklyn than a chic bistro in Saigon.

Peter came by often to check on us and see how we were doing. And when it finally came down to dessert, he explained each of the dishes, what they were, what their inspiration was, and so on. I learned as much as I enjoyed the food I ate. We then went up to the rooftop bar, where the view was nice and the breeze refreshing. There are quieter areas and louder areas up on the roof to suit every sort of taste. Though I did not have a cocktail myself, my friends were fawning over their drinks, yet another sign of Anan's creativity in gastronomy and mixology.
